hints: Think about the direction each gas must move in the lungs: which way should oxygen go, and which way should carbon dioxide go?
Gases diffuse down their partial pressure gradient, from high to low. Check each row to see if O2 is higher in alveolar air than in blood, and CO2 is higher in blood than in alveolar air.
walkthrough:
**Remember what has to happen in the lungs**

Blood arriving at the lungs is deoxygenated. It needs to pick up oxygen and get rid of carbon dioxide.

So we need: $O_2$ alveoli to blood, and $CO_2$ blood to alveoli.

**Use the diffusion rule**

Diffusion is always down a gradient, from higher partial pressure to lower partial pressure.

For $O_2$ to enter blood: $O_2$ in alveolar air must be greater than $O_2$ in blood.

For $CO_2$ to leave blood: $CO_2$ in blood must be greater than $CO_2$ in alveolar air.

**Check the numbers**

Correct gradients are about $13.9 \text{ kPa} > 5.3 \text{ kPa}$ for oxygen, and $6.0 \text{ kPa} > 5.3 \text{ kPa}$ for carbon dioxide.

Only option B has both gradients in the right direction, so both gases can diffuse correctly.

options.A: CO2 gradient is correct, but O2 in blood (13.9 kPa) is higher than in alveoli (13.3 kPa), so O2 would not diffuse into the blood.
options.B: CO2 is higher in blood (6.0 kPa) than alveoli (5.3 kPa) so it diffuses out, and O2 is higher in alveoli (13.9 kPa) than blood (5.3 kPa) so it diffuses in.
options.C: O2 gradient is correct, but CO2 in alveoli (6.0 kPa) is higher than in blood (5.3 kPa), so CO2 would not diffuse out of the blood.
options.D: Both gradients are backwards, CO2 is higher in alveoli and O2 is higher in blood, so neither gas would move in the needed direction.
